https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-south-kore.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nbon The North Korean soldiers, seen here in photos taken at a POW camp in Ukraine last February, had expressed a wish to resettle in South Korea Image: Kim Hong-Ji/REUTERS Advertisement Speaking at the UN General Assembly on September 23, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sparked a diplomatic dust-up with South Korea . In his speech, Zelenskyy mentioned that Ukraine had recently "sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea" — men who had been captured by Ukrainian forces during fighting in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025 . Both had expressed a wish to resettle in South Korea, he said. The reaction from Seoul was swift : South Korea's Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador to Seoul, Andrii Vieshkin, and demanded an explanation for what it described as Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the prisoners' transfer, despite a prior agreement to keep the matter confidential, along with an official apology. Russia's war in Ukraine has given North Korea the opportunity to strengthen ties with Moscow, in part by sending soldiers to the battlefield Image: KCNA/KNS/AFP Responding to Zelenskyy's speech, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war was a sensitive topic with wide-ranging consequences for diplomacy and national security on the Korean Peninsula. Did Kyiv and Seoul have a secret agreement? Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's spokesperson, wrote on Facebook that no such confidentiality agreement existed between the two countries, adding that it was wrong to keep secret where such prisoners were being transferred. Soon after, South Korean presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan called Lytvyn's denials false, according to news agency Reuters. Kim said Ukraine had asked for confidentiality — allegedly over concerns there might be criticism at home if the North Korean prisoners weren't swapped for Ukrainian prisoners being held in Russia . Seoul had agreed to the secrecy for diplomatic reasons, he added, but also to protect the prisoners and their families who were still living in North Korea . Missed opportunity to 'improve bilateral relations' Nataliya Butyrska, an Asia-Pacific expert at the New Europe Center in Kyiv, told DW that Ukraine and South Korea lacked a continuous, trust-based dialogue, especially under the current government in Seoul. "We should actually be natural partners — we should be standing shoulder to shoulder, with North Korea fighting against Ukraine," she said. "But that's not the case, due to a lack of trust." Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The prisoner transfer has been a hotly debated topic in South Korean media in the last week — not least because, according to South Korea's constitution, North Koreans are considered citizens of South Korea. It's also been instrumentalized by opposition lawmakers, while President Lee, aiming to ease tensions with the North, has taken a more measured approach. "The prisoners could have been used by Ukraine to improve bilateral relations between Kyiv and Seoul," said Butyrska, adding that no one in South Korea was now thinking of thanking Ukraine for transferring the prisoners. Butyrska pointed out that Russia, which usually doesn't express any interest in foreign prisoners , had actually demanded the return of these two North Koreans. "There was even a period of six months when the Russians refused to release any Ukrainian prisoners of war," she said. "They were not prepared to undertake any swap, because they wanted the North Koreans." Is Ukraine being held hostage by South Korea's domestic politics? For some observers, the diplomatic crisis can be linked back to domestic conflicts in South Korea. The opposition wants to know why the president agreed to keep the prisoner transfer secret, and have accused Lee of trying to gain favor with the North . "President Lee Jae Myung was surprised by the incident, and now wants to shift the blame in part on Ukraine," said Mykola Polishchuk, a Korea expert based in Ukraine. He believes the transfer would have become public knowledge sooner or later, and that Seoul knew that Kyiv was going to comment on it. Reports that Ukraine had asked for secrecy were, he added, a way for a frantic politicians in Seoul to come up with an explanation. "Ukraine has ended up mired in a scandal which it neither wanted nor planned for," said Polishchuk. North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "South Korea has been pursuing the transfer of the prisoners for a long time. And now everybody seems to be happy that those Korean prisoners are in custody," said Shim Sangmin from the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul. "But what really complicates the matter is the fact that the South Korean government is trying to make new ways to reconcile with the North Korean regime." He said Seoul was now worried that this transfer of North Korean prisoners could hamper efforts to reestablish communication between the North and the South . In his view, the Lee government is "more open to the idea of reestablishing ties" with Russia, rather than continuing to cooperate with Ukraine. "That's possibly one of the reasons why this government is skeptical about containing military cooperation with Ukrainian military forces, even though there would be a definite military advantage for South Korean military forces," he added. Ukraine shouldn't expect military support from South Korea Butyrska said the latest developments indicate a likely further cooling of ties between Kyiv and Seoul. "The South Korean government wasn't particularly friendly toward us to begin with, and will now likely keep its distance," she said, adding that it would have been better for Kyiv to have stayed quiet. In return for a gesture of goodwill and "quiet diplomacy," she added, Ukraine might have seen support from South Korea in another form — technology, for example, especially via third countries. While South Korea isn't directly selling weapons to Ukraine, it does deliver to Poland, Finland, the Czech Republic and Romania, and it's pursuing further integration with the European military equipment supply chain. For Polishchuk, any cooperation on military technology between Ukraine and South Korea is out of the question, now and in the future. He believes trade and humanitarian help would continue, however. South Korea, he said, is highly unlikely to side with Russia, especially given Seoul's many obligations toward the United States. This article was originally written in Ukrainian. https://telex.hu/g7/penz/2026/10/28/szja.text: Menü Kereső Az észt adórendszerhez fog hasonlítani a magyar az szja-jóváírás bevezetésével Pénz A kép illusztráció – Fotó: Mészáros János / MTI Stubnya Bence Az adójóváírás 2027-től várható bevezetése miatt az szja-kedvezmények rendszere is átalakulhat, ha az Országgyűlés elfogadja a törvényjavaslatot. A kedvezmények ezentúl közvetlenül a fizetendő adót csökkentenék – írja a Hvg.hu . Az adójóváírás bevezetéséről szóló törvénytervezet egyértelművé teszi a kedvezmények érvényesítésének sorrendjét: elsőként az adójóváírást kell levonni a fizetendő személyi jövedelemadóból, majd az így fennmaradó összegből érvényesíthetők a további adókedvezmények. A kedvezményeket a következő sorrendben lehet érvényesíteni: először a három vagy több gyermeket nevelő anyák, majd a 40 év alatti kétgyermekes anyák, a 30 év alatti anyák és a 25 év alatti fiatalok kedvezménye következik az adójóváírás után. Ezek után a személyi kedvezmény, az első házasok kedvezménye és a tevékenységi kedvezmény érvényesíthető, végül pedig a családi kedvezmény. Előzmények : Magyarországon 2011 előtt többkulcsos szja volt, amin belül azonban folyamatosan csökkent a kulcsok száma. 1996-ban még hétkulcsos rendszer volt, ez 2005-re kétkulcsosra csökkent, és 2010-ig így is maradt (amikor a felső kulcs 32, az alsó 17 százalékos volt). A minimálbér után az adójóváírás miatt 2002 és 2011 között nem kellett szja-t fizetni. A 16 százalékos egykulcsos adót a második Fidesz-kormány vezette be 2011-től, ez 2016-ban csökkent 15 százalékra, és azóta is ennyi maradt. Az adójóváírással az új kormány a mediánbér alatt keresők szja-terhelését csökkentené: a minimálbért keresőknek havi közel 20 ezer forintos, a minimálbér és a mediánbér között keresőknek pedig fokozatosan csökkenő összegű adókedvezményt biztosítana. Felülnézet : a tágabb régió 25 országából 11-ben van egykulcsos adó a Forvis Mazars Közép- és kelet-európai adókalauz 2026-os kiadása szerint (Bosznia-Hercegovina, Bulgária, Észtország, Kirgizisztán, Magyarország, Moldova, Észak-Macedónia, Románia, Szerbia, Ukrajna és Üzbegisztán). Az Európai Unióban jelenleg négy tagállamban van egykulcsos szja (Bulgária, Észtország, Magyarország, Románia), de ezen belül az észt nem tisztán egykulcsos, ott ugyanis adójóváírás vonatkozik a legalacsonyabb jövedelmekre. Magyarországon a munkát terhelő adózás progresszivitása a legalacsonyabb volt a Gazdasági Együttműködési és Fejlesztési Szervezet (OECD) tagállamai között az egyedülálló, gyermektelen munkavállalók esetében – ez derült ki a szervezet legfrissebb, 2026-os béreket terhelő adókról szóló kiadványából . Tágabb kontextus: a magyar szja legmagasabb kulcsa az adójóváírás jövő évi bevezetése után is 15 százalék marad, ami a Tax Foundation Europe által vizsgált 35 európai ország mezőnyében a 32. legalacsonyabb. Az összes munkára rakódó adóterhet figyelembe véve a hazai adóterhelés az OECD-átlag felett volt (35 és 41 százalék). Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

Composite: Amy Batey-McManus/Guardian Design/Supplied/Getty Images New South Wales Analysis As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals Anne Davies The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Fri 20 Nov 2026 09.00 EST Last modified on Fri 20 Nov 2026 09.02 EST Share The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore. This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament. The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether. As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”. Mark Speakman resigns and says Liberals face ‘existential threat’ as NSW exodus continues Read more But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns. This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin. Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote. “Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.” She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa , a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency. Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin. The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him. Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson. Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned. View image in fullscreen NSW opposition leader Kellie Sloane has not ruled out a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation. Photograph: Sarah Wilson/AAP At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished . The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents. “We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said. This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns . Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government. Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy. But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets. A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed. NSW’s latest news Instagram account has an unlikely group behind it: the Labor party Read more In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast. If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga. Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions. But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters. One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens. NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters. The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them. Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.
